result:
The instruction is simple: write whatever comes to you. It’s a deceptively heavy canvas, a blankness that demands to be filled but offers no clue as to what should fill it. It’s the tyranny of absolute freedom. For a moment, my mind is a frantic, silent static, a thousand possibilities clamoring for the exit at once, creating a traffic jam of thought. I could write about the squirrel I saw this morning, a twitchy ball of audacity perched on the fire escape, chattering down at the indifferent city. I could write about the faint, almost imperceptible hum of the refrigerator, the reliable heartbeat of a quiet apartment. I could write about the ache in my left knee, a souvenir from a fall I took years ago, a small, permanent footnote in the story of my body.

But those are just things. Objects and sensations. What comes to me now, as I settle into the rhythm of the keyboard, is a memory of a different kind of blankness. It was the first day of a writing workshop I took in my early twenties, full of naive ambition and a desperate hope to be seen as a “real” writer. The instructor, a wry, silver-haired man named Leo who smelled of coffee and old books, had given us the same prompt. “Write for an hour,” he’d said, tapping his watch. “No stopping. No editing. Just let it come.”

I remember the panic. The same static, the same traffic jam. For the first ten minutes, I wrote a terrible, derivative poem about the rain. Then I wrote a paragraph of a story that went nowhere, a character with no name or purpose. I could feel Leo’s presence in the room, his slow, ambling pace as he circled our tables. I was certain he would stop and look over my shoulder, see the embarrassing mess on the page, and politely suggest I consider a career in accounting. But he never did. He just walked and let us be.

And then, something shifted. I ran out of things to *try* to write. I had exhausted the beginnings of every half-baked idea I had ever had. And in that moment of giving up, something else took over. I started writing about the act of writing itself. About the pressure, the fear, the feeling of being an impostor. I wrote about the texture of the paper, the slight scratch of the pen. I wrote about the other people in the room: the woman next to me with the furious pace of someone trying to outrun a demon, the man across the table who would stop and stare at the ceiling for what felt like minutes.

And from there, a different story emerged. It wasn't a grand narrative, but a small, true one. It was about a boy who collected lost buttons. He kept them in an old mint tin, each one a mystery. He’d imagine the coats they belonged to, the people who wore them, the lives they lived. A brass button from a soldier’s uniform. A delicate glass one from a woman’s evening gown. A simple wooden toggle from a child’s duffle coat. For an hour, I lived in the world of that tin, sorting through the stories, giving each button a history. It was the most honest thing I had written in years.

When Leo called time, I felt a strange sense of loss. I had been somewhere else, a place I hadn't known existed. It was a space discovered only by running through the wall of the expected.

That’s what writing feels like to me now. It’s the process of finding that lost button. You start with the overwhelming blankness, the cacophony of choices. You try a few things that feel wrong, that are forced, that are echoes of other people's voices. And then, if you’re lucky and you’re patient, and you’re willing to be a little bored or a little scared, the noise fades. A single, quiet voice emerges. It’s not the loudest one, or the cleverest one. It’s the one that has been there all along, waiting for you to stop shouting so it could be heard.

I think about the world and its relentless demands for meaning. We are asked to have opinions, to take stands, to summarize complex realities into neat, shareable packages. We are a species obsessed with conclusions, with the tidy moral at the end of the fable. But the act of writing—the real act—is a rebellion against that. It’s a space for nuance, for ambiguity, for the exploration of a feeling without having to justify it. It’s a place where a collection of lost buttons can be as meaningful as a political treatise, because it’s a vessel for a moment of true, unadorned human attention.

So now, with 1000 words stretching out before me, I find myself back in that workshop room. The frantic static has subsided. The world has quieted down. I’m not trying to write something profound or important. I’m just trying to pay attention. To the hum of the refrigerator, the ghost of a fall, the memory of a silver-haired man and a tin of buttons. I am trying to let something come, and to trust that the act of building a bridge, one word after another, into the vast, empty space, is a meaningful thing to do, even if I don’t know where the other side will land. The space is no longer blank. It is full of everything that is, and everything that has been, and everything that just might be.
